# Arctic Blast Grips Upper Midwest and Great Lakes as Temperatures Plunge to Dangerous Lows

**By CNN Staff**

A brutal arctic cold front has descended upon the upper Midwest and Great Lakes region this week, sending temperatures plummeting to life-threatening lows and prompting emergency warnings across multiple states.

## Record-Breaking Temperatures

The National Weather Service reported that temperatures across the region have plunged well below zero, with wind chills making conditions even more dangerous.

International Falls, Minnesota—often called the "Icebox of the Nation"—recorded a bone-chilling minus 38 degrees Fahrenheit early Wednesday morning, with wind chills approaching minus 55. Minneapolis saw actual temperatures of minus 22, while Duluth registered minus 27.

The frigid conditions extended eastward, with Green Bay, Wisconsin, dropping to minus 18 and Marquette, Michigan, along Lake Superior, hitting minus 21. Chicago wasn't spared, with the Windy City living up to its name as temperatures fell to minus 11 with wind chills near minus 30.

## Communities Respond to the Crisis

Cities across the affected region have opened emergency warming centers and are urging residents to check on vulnerable neighbors.

"This is the kind of cold that can kill you in minutes if you're not prepared," said Minneapolis Emergency Management Director Sarah Chen. "We're seeing wind chills that can cause frostbite on exposed skin in under 10 minutes."

## Personal Stories from the Front Lines

For Marcus Thompson, a 34-year-old mail carrier in St. Paul, the cold has made his daily route grueling. "I've got three layers on plus hand warmers in my gloves, and I'm still freezing," Thompson said. "You just keep moving and try to get done as fast as you safely can."

Eleanor Rodriguez, 72, who lives alone in Milwaukee, said the cold has left her housebound. "My daughter called to make sure I had enough groceries and that my heat was working," Rodriguez said. "I'm afraid to even step outside. At my age, a fall on the ice in this weather could be deadly."

Local shelters have seen increased demand. James Whitmore, who volunteers at a Chicago warming center, described the scene: "We've had people coming in all night. Some folks don't have anywhere warm to go, and in this weather, we can literally be the difference between life and death."

Farmers have faced their own challenges. Dairy farmer Rebecca Olson near Eau Claire, Wisconsin, has been working around the clock to protect her livestock. "We've got heaters running in the barn and we're checking the animals constantly," Olson said. "The cattle need extra feed just to maintain their body heat, and keeping the water from freezing is a full-time job."

## Widespread Disruptions

The extreme cold has caused significant disruptions across the region:

- **Schools closed:** Dozens of school districts across Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Michigan canceled classes to protect students from dangerous conditions.

- **Travel troubles:** Hundreds of flights were delayed or canceled at Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport and Chicago's O'Hare. Officials warned that car batteries and engines are particularly vulnerable in such extreme cold.

- **Power concerns:** Utility companies urged residents to conserve energy as demand surged, though no major outages had been reported as of Wednesday afternoon.

## Health Warnings

Medical professionals are warning residents about the serious health risks posed by the extreme cold.

"We're seeing cases of frostbite and hypothermia," said Dr. Michael Barnes, an emergency physician at a Minneapolis hospital. "People need to understand that this weather is genuinely dangerous. Cover all exposed skin, limit time outdoors, and never leave children or pets in vehicles."

Officials also reminded pet owners to bring animals indoors, as the conditions are equally dangerous for animals.

## The Forecast Ahead

Meteorologists say relief is on the way, though not immediately.

According to the National Weather Service, the coldest temperatures will persist through Thursday, with overnight lows remaining well below zero across the region. A gradual warming trend is expected to begin Friday.

"We'll see temperatures start to moderate by the weekend," said CNN meteorologist Dana Foster. "By Saturday, highs could climb back into the teens and 20s, which will feel almost balmy compared to what people have been experiencing."

However, forecasters caution that the warming could bring its own hazards, including the potential for snow as a new system moves through early next week.

Officials continue to urge residents to stay indoors when possible, dress in layers if venturing out, and remain vigilant about the risks of the extreme cold.

*This is a developing story and will be updated.*

---

*CNN's weather team contributed to this report.*

# Arctic Blast Grips Midwest as Alberta Clipper Delivers Record Cold, Claims One Life

*Bitter temperatures shatter records across multiple states; officials warn of dangerous conditions through weekend*

**CHICAGO** — A fast-moving Alberta clipper storm system swept across the Upper Midwest this week, plunging temperatures to record-breaking lows, sending dozens to hospitals with frostbite and hypothermia, and contributing to at least one death as the region grappled with some of the most dangerous winter conditions in years.

The storm, which originated in the Canadian province of Alberta before racing southeast, brought a punishing combination of light snow, fierce winds, and rapidly dropping temperatures that caught some residents off guard despite advance warnings from the National Weather Service.

## Record Temperatures Fall

By early Thursday morning, thermometers across the region told a stark story. International Falls, Minnesota, often dubbed the "Icebox of the Nation," recorded minus 41 degrees Fahrenheit, breaking a record that had stood since 1967. Minneapolis-St. Paul reached minus 28 degrees, while wind chills across parts of Minnesota, Wisconsin, and North Dakota plummeted to between minus 50 and minus 60 degrees.

"This is the kind of cold that turns dangerous within minutes, not hours," said Dr. Sarah Whitfield, an emergency medicine physician at a Minneapolis hospital. "At these wind chills, exposed skin can develop frostbite in as little as five to ten minutes."

The National Weather Service issued wind chill warnings spanning seven states, urging residents to remain indoors and avoid unnecessary travel.

## A Life Lost

The storm's most tragic consequence came in rural Wisconsin, where authorities confirmed the death of a 67-year-old man found outside his home late Wednesday. According to the county sheriff's office, the man had apparently gone outside to check on a generator during a brief power outage and was unable to return indoors.

"Our hearts go out to the family," said Sheriff's Deputy Marcus Reyes at a press briefing. "This is a painful reminder that these temperatures don't offer second chances. We're asking everyone to check on elderly neighbors and relatives."

The victim's name was withheld pending notification of family members.

## Hospitals See Surge in Cold-Related Injuries

Emergency rooms across the region reported a sharp increase in patients suffering from frostbite and hypothermia. At least 40 people sought treatment for cold-related injuries in the Twin Cities metropolitan area alone, hospital officials said.

Many of the affected were homeless individuals, stranded motorists, or people who underestimated the severity of the conditions.

"We've seen everything from mild frostnip to severe frostbite requiring potential amputation," Dr. Whitfield said. "The tissue damage from this kind of cold can be devastating and permanent."

Homeless outreach organizations scrambled to expand shelter capacity. In Chicago, warming centers extended their hours around the clock, and city officials deployed additional buses as mobile warming stations.

"Nobody should have to face this weather without shelter," said Deborah Klein, director of a Chicago-based homeless services nonprofit. "We're doing everything we can to get people inside."

## Transportation Snarled

While Alberta clippers typically produce only light snow, the accompanying winds created ground blizzards in open rural areas, reducing visibility and making travel treacherous.

The Minnesota Department of Transportation reported multiple vehicle spinouts and closures on stretches of Interstate 94. Several school districts across Minnesota, Wisconsin, and the Dakotas canceled classes or shifted to remote learning for a second consecutive day.

Air travel also suffered, with hundreds of flights delayed or canceled at Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport and Chicago's O'Hare International Airport as ground crews battled to keep operations running in the punishing cold.

## Understanding the Alberta Clipper

Meteorologists explained that Alberta clippers are fast-moving low-pressure systems that draw their name from their point of origin and their swift, "clipper ship" movement across the continent.

"These systems don't usually bring heavy snow, but they're notorious for dragging down bitterly cold Arctic air behind them," said meteorologist James Portillo. "It's that trailing cold front that creates the real danger — the temperature crash and the wind chill."

Portillo noted that the current system was reinforced by a lobe of the polar vortex dipping unusually far south, amplifying the cold.

## Looking Ahead

Forecasters expect the dangerous cold to persist through the weekend before a gradual moderation begins early next week. In the meantime, officials continue to urge caution.

Authorities recommend that residents:

- Limit time outdoors and dress in layers with minimal exposed skin
- Check on elderly and vulnerable neighbors
- Keep emergency kits, blankets, and phone chargers in vehicles
- Never run generators or grills indoors due to carbon monoxide risks
- Bring pets inside

"The bottom line is simple," Deputy Reyes said. "Respect the cold. Stay inside if you can. And look out for one another."

As the region hunkers down against the relentless chill, communities across the Midwest are bracing for several more days of a winter that has already proven both record-setting and deadly.

*This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.*

## A Fatal Night

In suburban Milwaukee, tragedy struck when 68-year-old Harold Jennings, a retired postal worker, was found dead outside his home early Tuesday morning. Authorities believe Jennings, who had a documented history of sleepwalking, wandered out of his house in the middle of the night and was unable to get back inside.

"He'd struggled with sleepwalking for years, but nothing like this ever happened before," said his daughter, Karen Jennings, her voice breaking during a phone interview. "The door locked behind him. He was in his pajamas. By the time anyone realized he was gone, it was already too late."

The medical examiner's preliminary findings listed hypothermia as the cause of death. Overnight temperatures in the area had dropped to 18 below zero.

Local officials used the death as a somber warning. "This is exactly the kind of tragedy we're trying to prevent," said a county sheriff's spokesperson. "Check on your elderly neighbors. Check on family members who might be vulnerable. A few minutes of caring could save a life."

## The Cost of a Moment Outside

For 34-year-old Marcus Bell of Detroit, a routine morning turned into a medical emergency. After his car stalled on a highway shoulder, Bell spent roughly 40 minutes waiting for roadside assistance—much of it outside his vehicle attempting to flag down help.

He is now being treated for severe frostbite on several fingers.

"I didn't think it was that bad. I had gloves on, but they were thin," Bell said from his hospital bed, his bandaged hands resting on a blanket. "By the time the tow truck came, I couldn't feel my hands at all. The doctors are telling me they're trying to save all my fingers, but they don't know yet."

Bell's physician, speaking generally about cold-weather injuries, said hospitals across the region had seen a spike in frostbite and hypothermia cases. "People underestimate how fast this happens," the doctor said. "In these conditions, exposed skin doesn't have much time. We're urging everyone to cover every inch."

## Workers Brave the Elements

While most residents heeded warnings to stay home, thousands of essential workers had no choice but to face the cold.

At a rail yard outside Chicago, maintenance workers bundled in multiple layers worked in short shifts to keep switches from freezing.

"You can only stay out there fifteen, twenty minutes before you've gotta come in and warm up," said Danny Ruiz, a track maintenance worker with more than a decade of experience. "The metal gets so cold it burns you right through your gloves. I've never felt anything like this year."

Nearby, snowplow operator Terrence Wallace was midway through a 12-hour shift clearing city streets. "We don't get to call in sick from weather—we *are* the response to the weather," Wallace said with a tired laugh. "My biggest worry isn't me, it's the folks whose cars break down. You see somebody stranded out here in this, it's scary."

Utility crews also remained on high alert as demand for heating pushed power grids to their limits. A spokesperson for a regional energy provider urged customers to conserve energy where possible and report outages immediately.

As if the frigid temperatures weren't enough, a fresh round of snowfall is expected to blanket much of the region over the next 48 hours. Forecasters have issued winter storm warnings across multiple states.

The deep freeze forced widespread disruptions. Hundreds of schools announced closures, airlines canceled or delayed more than a thousand flights at major hubs including O'Hare International Airport, and cities opened emergency warming centers for people experiencing homelessness.

"We've expanded capacity at every shelter we have," said a director at a Chicago-based homeless services organization. "Nobody should have to be outside in this. Nobody."

Meteorologists offered a glimmer of hope, predicting that the Arctic air mass would begin to retreat by the weekend, with temperatures gradually climbing back toward seasonal norms early next week.

Until then, the message from officials remains unwavering.

"Stay inside. Stay warm. Check on the people you love," the Weather Service meteorologist said. "This cold is dangerous, and it's not done with us yet."
